Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Guinea-Bissau predominantly use paper-based recording for patient data. The 2016 Health Sector Diagnostic states: "The majority of health centers don't have automated process. All data is registered on forms and books, with a logical sequence and order; however, there is not a preservation mechanisms or control of the quality of registration." The 2019 World Bank Service Delivery Indicators (SDI) Health report notes "non-operational health-information systems" and relies on manual outpatient records for caseloads, with no mentions of digital tools at point-of-care in surveyed facilities (62% rural). No evidence found of routine electronic health records (EHR) or DHIS2 use at rural clinics for patient registration; DHIS2 is national-level for aggregate reporting/surveillance since ~2018, with data likely paper-collected then transcribed at district level. Isolated NGO pilots (e.g., DREAM HIV software, Clinic+O community digital tools in Guinea-not Bissau) exist but do not represent standard practice. Key barriers: poor infrastructure (45% facilities have basic electricity/water/sanitation), lack of computers/internet in rural areas, insufficient trained staff, political instability. National ambitions include DHIS2 expansion and recent platforms (e.g., NIA 2026), but rural point-of-service remains paper-based, with large gap between policy and reality.

revision_notes: Original cited sources (2016 Health Sector Diagnostic, 2019 SDI report, 2020 DHIS2 blog) verified and confirm paper-based data capture at rural clinics. A fresh check finds DHIS2 in use nationally since 2011/2014 for malaria and other aggregate reporting across around 145 facilities, and a May 2024 Zenysis/INASA/MINSAP partnership announcement explicitly cites reliance on manual, error-prone data entry as the current baseline problem, confirming the score. DHIS2 entries are aggregate/district-level reporting rather than point-of-care digital capture at the clinic, consistent with metadata guidance to exclude higher-level digitalisation. Score of 1 (Entirely paper) confirmed.
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Guinea-Bissau continue to rely on paper-based recording of patient data at the point of care. Guinea-Bissau has used the DHIS2 platform since 2011 for national health information management, and Global Fund-supported digitisation covers around 145 facilities for malaria and other disease surveillance, but this operates as aggregate district-level reporting rather than digital record-keeping within the clinic itself. A May 2024 partnership between INASA, MINSAP and Zenysis Technologies to build a National Integration and Analytics Platform explicitly identifies manual, error-prone data entry across more than twenty fragmented health data systems as the current baseline challenge, with over 60 percent of systems inaccessible to INASA management. No evidence indicates routine electronic patient records or digital data capture at the rural clinic level.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: No direct evidence on rural police stations, but justice sector shows early digital pilots (e.g., SIGDAJ for MoJ data aggregation, Judiciary Police judicial forum website, online complaint submission on pj.gw with case tracking Polícia Judiciária). UNDP E-Justice (2023) notes shift from paper-based methods, targeting regional decentralization, implying predominantly paper at rural/outlying stations with central digital entry/pilots. UNODC goCASE (2014) limited to urban TCU. Model station in rural Gabú (2024 UNODC/UNDP) focuses on community policing infrastructure, no records tech mentioned. Lacks evidence of predominant digital at station level; fits score 2 per rules (pilots/donor projects).

revision_notes: Original comment text argued the evidence fits score 2 while the recorded Value Code was left at 1, an internal inconsistency. On review, the cited and fresh sources concern the Ministry of Justice SIGDAJ pilot and e-justice tests in tribunals and CAJ offices (not police stations), the Judiciary Police national web portal (pj.gw, an urban/headquarters complaint-tracking system), and the UNODC goCASE system deployed only at the urban Transnational Crime Unit. None relate to record capture at rural police stations. The 2024 UNDP Annual Report profile of the Gabu Model Police Station (a rural facility opened in 2024) describes infrastructure, staffing and community-policing improvements but makes no mention of digital records systems. No evidence of any digitisation of record-keeping at rural police stations was found; score 1 (Entirely paper) confirmed and the Value Code/Comments inconsistency resolved in favour of 1.
revised_comments: Rural police stations in Guinea-Bissau continue to rely on paper-based record-keeping. Digital initiatives identified in the country's justice and security sector, such as the Ministry of Justice SIGDAJ case-management pilot, the Judiciary Police national online complaint portal (pj.gw), and the UNODC goCASE system, are concentrated at the Ministry of Justice, the judiciary and the urban Transnational Crime Unit rather than at rural police stations. The Gabu Model Police Station, a rural facility developed with UN Peacebuilding Fund support and opened in 2024, has introduced community-policing practices, gender-responsive training and dedicated facilities for women, but no digital records system for policing data has been identified at rural stations.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices in Guinea-Bissau rely entirely on paper-based recording for births and vital events. UNICEF data confirms civil registration processing is manual (on paper), with new services at health facilities but no digital tools at point of service [UNICEF CRVS]. Low rural birth registration completeness (17.5% in 2014 MICS per World Bank, likely similar recently) reflects access barriers, not digitalization [World Bank rural data]. A national SIREC digital system began in 2025 for digitizing records and some birth registrations, supported by UNDP/UNICEF, with efforts to extend to remote areas and health facilities [Biometric Update]. However, as a recent pilot/early rollout (started ~3 months prior to June 2025), it represents isolated digital efforts, not standard at rural registries. Key barriers: poor infrastructure, low literacy, remoteness, funding shortages. National ambition for digital CRVS exists, but rural point-of-service remains paper-based with data later aggregated digitally if at all. No evidence majority rural facilities use digital routinely.

revision_notes: Original sources (UNICEF CRVS profile, World Bank rural birth registration completeness data, June 2025 Biometric Update interview) confirm that civil registration in Guinea-Bissau was historically entirely paper-based and that a new digital system (SIREC) was only beginning rollout as of mid-2025. Fresh sources on the SIREC launch (Aveiro University, January 2025; UNDP Guinea-Bissau 2024 Annual Report) show the system went live on 23 January 2025 at the 1st Conservatoria in Bissau, that it is EU-funded and includes birth, marriage and death modules, and that a mobile registration vehicle has been provided specifically to extend digital registration to remote regions. The UNDP report also records 7,500 registry books and 1.3 million civil acts digitised across five regions (though this is retrospective archive digitisation rather than new-record capture) and training of civil registry officers in the use of digital enrollment kits, including efforts to register births at health facilities. Given the genuine, government-led transition now under way and specifically targeting rural and remote registration, the status is revised upward from Entirely paper to Mostly paper - some digital (2). A promotion to Entirely digital (4) or even Mostly digital (3) is not supported, since the rollout began only in 2025, is still concentrated in Bissau, and rural coverage via mobile units remains nascent.
revised_comments: Civil registration in rural Guinea-Bissau is transitioning from an entirely paper-based system towards partial digital capture. The new SIREC (Integrated Citizen Registration and Statistics System), an EU-funded platform developed with the University of Aveiro and Portugal's Institute of Registries and Notaries, went live in January 2025 at the first Conservatoria in Bissau, with modules covering birth, marriage and death registration. A mobile registration vehicle has been deployed to extend SIREC-based registration to remote regions, and civil registry officers have received training in the use of digital enrollment kits, including registering births at health facilities. As of mid-2025 the rollout remains recent and concentrated on the capital, with only around 46 percent of children under five registered nationally and extension to remote rural registries still under way, so most rural civil registry offices continue to rely predominantly on paper, with digital capture emerging alongside it.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in Guinea-Bissau operate under severe constraints: pupil-teacher ratio of 51.9:1, only 25% of primary schools offer full 6 grades (mostly urban), frequent teacher strikes, low infrastructure in rural areas (60% population rural). No evidence of digital recording of attendance, enrollment, grades at school level. Recent World Bank/GPE projects introduced electronic surveys to principals (GEMS-based) and Kobo Toolbox for inspectors in 5 targeted regions-pilots for aggregate stats/monitoring, not routine school data. No operational EMIS; historical absence of regular assessments. Data collection likely paper-based at rural facilities, aggregated centrally if at all. Score 1: entirely paper-based, consistent with low-income African rural norms absent specific digital evidence. (148 words)

revision_notes: Original sources (UNESCO IICBA country brief, World Bank Quality Education project ISR, EPDC national education profile) confirm chronic capacity constraints (51.9 to 1 pupil-teacher ratio, only 25 percent of primary schools offering all 6 grades) but do not evidence digital record capture at school level. A fresh search finds recent monitoring initiatives, including the World Bank GEMS programme which digitised school inspections for near-real-time oversight, the PRIEQT/World Bank/UNICEF 2024 nationwide school-mapping exercise using Kobo Toolbox, and the EU-financed PESIDE project developing the SIGE education-management platform at regional level, but these all involve inspectors, enumerators or regional offices collecting or digitising data about schools, not schools themselves capturing attendance, enrolment or grade records digitally at the facility. Per the metadata guidance to exclude higher-level digitalisation of paper data, the status remains Entirely paper (1). The most recent, most directly relevant data point is the PASEC 2024 assessment, whose data collection took place in May 2025 across all 11 regions, again gathered by external survey teams rather than through school-level digital systems.
revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Guinea-Bissau continue to keep attendance, enrolment and grade records on paper. Severe capacity constraints persist, including a pupil-teacher ratio of around 52 to 1 and only about a quarter of primary schools offering the full six-grade cycle. Recent education-data initiatives, including the World Bank GEMS-supported digitisation of school inspections, a 2024 nationwide school-mapping exercise conducted with Kobo Toolbox under the PRIEQT project, the EU-financed PESIDE project building a regional education-management information system (SIGE), and the 2024/25 PASEC learning assessment, involve external enumerators, inspectors or regional education offices collecting and digitising data about schools, rather than schools themselves maintaining digital records at the point of data capture. No evidence indicates that rural primary schools record attendance or academic data digitally at the facility level.
